mainTopic: Partners' rights in a shared courtyard (חזקה, laundry), guarding one's eyes, and the dress and table of a תלמיד חכם.
overview: The גמרא first explains why placing things in a courtyard is not a חזקה but building a מחיצה is. The first answer is that partners don't mind each other placing things. A משנה in נדרים seems to show that partners do mind. רב נחמן, רב פפא and רבינא each give a different answer to that challenge. Next, רבי יוחנן quotes רבי בנאה: partners can block each other from any use of a shared courtyard except laundry, to protect women's dignity. This leads to רבי חייא בר אבא's teaching that a man who shuts his eyes from evil is one who does not stare at women doing laundry, even when he has no other road. רבי בנאה then describes how a תלמיד חכם should dress and set his table. The גמרא settles a contradiction about where the table's ring goes in three different ways. The amud ends as the גמרא begins to describe the table of an עם הארץ, and the comparison continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The case is a courtyard owned by partners
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the case is a שותפין courtyard. Partners don't mind each other placing things there, but they do mind a partition.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are talking about a courtyard owned by partners. Partners don't care if the other one just puts things there, but they do care if he builds a partition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why placing things in the courtyard is not a חזקה, but building a מחיצה is. It does this by saying the case is a courtyard owned by partners.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חזקה only works when the other person's silence shows he agrees the property is no longer his. Partners normally don't mind each other just putting things in the shared courtyard, so staying quiet about it proves nothing. Building a מחיצה is different: partners do object to that, so silence there is meaningful.

keyTerms.meaning: A courtyard owned jointly by partners
Simply placing or keeping things (like animals) somewhere

phrases.english: Here we are dealing with a courtyard belonging to partners —
where they are not particular about merely placing things,
but about a partition they are particular.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from the previous section about why placing things is not a חזקה but a partition is.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא) to a partners' courtyard
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Placing items in someone's courtyard should count as a חזקה.
steps.terutzMaskana: In a partners' courtyard, placing items is not a חזקה, because partners don't mind it. A partition, which they do mind, is a חזקה.

steps.title: But partners do care, as the משנה about vows shows
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that partners don't mind. A משנה says partners who made a נדר against benefiting from each other may not even enter their shared courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do partners really not mind? We learned that partners who vowed not to benefit from each other may not enter their shared courtyard!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of step 1 using a משנה from מסכת נדרים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If partners who made a נדר may not even walk into their shared courtyard, then using the partner's share counts as a real benefit. That means each partner does mind. Putting animals or items there should be even more of a benefit than just walking in, so the claim that partners 'don't mind' seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't we learn in a משנה (introduces a challenge)

phrases.english: And are they really not particular about merely placing things?!
But didn't we learn in a משנה:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה in נדרים 45b.

phrases.english: Partners who vowed to forbid benefit from one another —
are forbidden to enter the courtyard!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבְהַעֲמָדָה כְּדִי לָא קָפְדִי וְהָא תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption in step 1 that partners don't mind each other placing things.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that partners are not particular about mere placing of items.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה in נדרים forbids even entering a shared courtyard, which shows partners care about each other's use of their share. Placing items should be no less than walking in.

steps.title: The case is a yard behind the houses
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן, quoting רבה בר אבוה, moves the case to a back yard behind the houses. There people don't mind items being placed, but they do mind a partition.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the case is a yard behind the houses. People don't mind things just being put there, but they do mind a partition.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the partners' courtyard answer was challenged, the גמרא gives a new setting: a back yard behind the houses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A back yard is not used much, so owners don't care if someone just leaves things there. That means silence about placing proves nothing. A מחיצה is a real change, so silence about it still counts. This avoids the problem from נדרים, which was about a regular partners' courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: An open yard or enclosed area

phrases.english: Rather, רב נחמן said
that רבה בר אבוה said:

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא בִּרְחָבָה שֶׁל אֲחוֹרֵי בָתִּים עָסְקִינַן;
phrases.english: Here we are dealing with a yard behind the houses;
where they are not particular about merely placing things,
but about a partition they are particular.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Drops the answer of step 1 because of the challenge in step 2, and offers a new setting.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case is a partners' courtyard, but the נדרים משנה shows partners do mind.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is a back yard behind houses, where nobody minds placing items. So placing is no חזקה, while a partition is.

steps.title: Some partners mind and some don't, so money and איסור are judged differently
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says both משניות are about a partners' courtyard. Since some partners mind and some don't, we rule leniently in money matters and strictly in איסור matters.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both cases are about a partners' courtyard. Some partners mind and some don't. For money we are lenient, and for prohibitions we are strict.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a different way to answer the challenge in step 2. He keeps the case as a partners' courtyard, as step 1 said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We don't know whether a given partner minds. In a money case like חזקה, we take the lenient view that he doesn't mind, so his silence about placing items proves nothing and no חזקה is made. In an איסור case like a נדר, we take the strict view that he does mind, so entering counts as benefit and is forbidden.
steps.confusionAlert: Here 'lenient' in money matters does not mean the person placing things wins. It means we assume the partner doesn't mind, so his silence proves nothing and placing items does not create a חזקה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common pattern in the גמרא: when we are unsure, money questions and איסור questions can get opposite results.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
Both this and that are about a partners' courtyard;
phrases.notes: 'This and that' means our משנה here and the משנה in נדרים.

phrases.english: and there are those who mind and those who don't mind;
regarding money matters — we go leniently,
regarding prohibitions — we go strictly.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בַּחֲצַר הַשּׁוּתָּפִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers another answer to step 2, different from step 3. It keeps the partners' courtyard setting from step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Resolving the contradiction by different rules for money and איסור
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The נדרים משנה proves that all partners mind, so they cannot be assumed not to mind here.
steps.terutzMaskana: Partners differ. In money matters we assume they don't mind (so there is no חזקה from placing), and in איסור matters we assume they do mind (so entering is forbidden).

steps.title: רבינא: partners don't mind, and the נדרים משנה follows רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: רבינא keeps the original idea that partners do not mind each other's use of the courtyard. He explains that the משנה in נדרים follows רבי אליעזר, who forbids even tiny benefits to someone under a מודר הנאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Really, partners are not particular. Whose view is that משנה? It is רבי אליעזר's. A ברייתא teaches that רבי אליעזר says: even small things people normally let go of are forbidden to someone who is vowed from benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives a third answer to the challenge from the משנה in נדרים. He does not change the case. He says that משנה follows one particular תנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge was: if partners don't mind, why can't partners under a נדר enter the shared courtyard? רבינא answers that רבי אליעזר forbids even ויתור, a benefit people usually give away freely. So the נדר forbids entering even though partners normally don't mind.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually; it signals that we keep the original position
A small benefit people normally give up freely
Someone forbidden by a vow from getting benefit from another person

steps.confusionAlert: רבינא is not saying partners do mind. He agrees they don't. He only explains that under רבי אליעזר's strict view, even benefits nobody cares about are forbidden to a מודר הנאה.

phrases.english: Ravina said: Actually, they are not particular,
and this one, whose view is it? It is Rabbi Eliezer's;
phrases.notes: "This one" is the משנה in נדרים about partners who vowed not to benefit from each other.

phrases.english: as it is taught: Rabbi Eliezer says:
even something people freely give up is forbidden for one vowed from benefit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to the challenge in step 2, after רב נחמן (step 3) and רב פפא (step 4).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the challenging משנה to a specific תנא (רבי אליעזר)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה in נדרים seemed to show that partners mind each other entering the courtyard.
steps.terutzMaskana: Partners don't mind. The משנה forbids entry only because רבי אליעזר forbids even ויתור to a מודר הנאה.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three answers to the challenge from נדרים. רב נחמן moves the case to a back yard behind the houses. רב פפא keeps it as a partners' courtyard: since partners differ, money matters are judged leniently and איסור matters strictly. רבינא says partners really don't mind, and the נדרים משנה follows רבי אליעזר, who forbids even ויתור.

steps.title: Partners can block each other from everything except laundry
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי בנאה, rules that each partner can stop the other from any use of the shared courtyard except doing laundry, so that Jewish women are not shamed by washing in public.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי בנאה: Partners can stop each other from any use, except laundry. It is not the way of Jewish women to be shamed by doing laundry in public.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement about partners in a shared courtyard. Laundry is the one use a partner cannot block.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general rule is that each partner can stop the other from using the shared yard. Laundry is an exception because the alternative is washing in a public place, which would embarrass the women. Their dignity outweighs the partner's right to object.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical rule for shared property: the partner's right to object has a limit when someone's dignity is at stake.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי בְּנָאָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Bena'a:

phrases.aramaic: בַּכֹּל שׁוּתָּפִין מְעַכְּבִין זֶה אֶת זֶה,
phrases.english: In everything, partners can prevent one another,
except for laundry –
since it is not the way of Jewish women
to be shamed over laundry.
phrases.notes: If they could not wash in the yard, they would have to do it out in public.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי בְּנָאָה: בַּכֹּל שׁוּתָּפִין מְעַכְּבִין זֶה אֶת זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the debate over whether partners mind to a new rule about what partners may stop each other from doing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Partners may block each other from any use of the courtyard except laundry, to protect women's dignity.

steps.title: Shutting one's eyes from evil: not staring at women doing laundry
steps.stepSummary: Because laundry came up, the גמרא quotes a פסוק praising someone who shuts his eyes from seeing evil. רבי חייא בר אבא says this means a man who does not stare at women while they do laundry.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And shuts his eyes from seeing evil." רבי חייא בר אבא said: This is someone who does not stare at women while they stand doing laundry.
steps.whatsHappening: The topic of laundry leads the גמרא to an aggadic teaching. It explains a פסוק about guarding one's eyes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק praises someone who shuts his eyes from evil. רבי חייא בר אבא applies it to a real situation: women doing laundry might be less fully covered. The praised person is one who does not look.

phrases.english: "And shuts his eyes from seeing evil" –
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said:
This is one who does not gaze at women
at the time they stand over the laundry.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעֹצֵם עֵינָיו מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע – אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Linked by topic: laundry in step 6 leads to this teaching about laundry.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק's praise of shutting one's eyes refers to not gazing at women while they do laundry.

steps.title: What is the case? Either he is wicked or he is helpless
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what situation רבי חייא בר אבא means. If the man had another route, walking past the women makes him wicked. If he had no other route, he is helpless, so why would he deserve special praise?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If there is another road, he is wicked! If there is no other road, he is forced!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests רבי חייא בר אבא's teaching with a two-sided question. Neither option seems to fit a case where the man earns praise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With another route, choosing to pass the women is already wrong, so shutting his eyes is not praiseworthy. With no other route, he has no choice, so it is unclear what he is praised for. The question sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? / How do we picture it?
Someone forced by circumstances, with no choice

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?

phrases.aramaic: אִי דְּאִיכָּא דַּרְכָּא אַחְרִיתָא – רָשָׁע הוּא!
phrases.english: If there is another road – he is wicked!

phrases.aramaic: אִי דְּלֵיכָּא דַּרְכָּא אַחְרִיתָא – אָנוּס הוּא!
phrases.english: If there is no other road – he is forced!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִי דְּאִיכָּא דַּרְכָּא אַחְרִיתָא – רָשָׁע הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the teaching in step 7 by asking what situation it describes.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא בר אבא's reading of the פסוק as praise for not looking at women doing laundry.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A two-sided question: with another road he is wicked for going that way, and without one he is helpless. Either way, it is hard to see what he is praised for.

steps.title: No other road, yet he must still force himself not to look
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that there really was no other road. Even so, he must force himself not to stare, and that effort is what the פסוק praises.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, there is no other road. Even so, he must force himself not to look.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 8 by choosing the second option and explaining why it still earns praise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having no choice about the route does not mean having no choice about where he looks. He must still force himself not to gaze, and that self-control is what the פסוק praises.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs to / he is required to

steps.whatToRemember: Partners can block each other from using a shared yard, except for laundry, to protect women's dignity. A man who must pass women doing laundry, with no other road, still has to force himself not to look. That is what "shuts his eyes from seeing evil" means.
steps.whyThisMatters: Being forced into a situation does not remove a person's duty to control himself within it.

phrases.english: Actually, it is where there is no other road,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי – מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְמֵינַס נַפְשֵׁיהּ.
phrases.english: and even so – he must force himself.
phrases.notes: He has to walk that way, but he still has to hold himself back from staring.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם דְּלֵיכָּא דַּרְכָּא אַחְרִיתָא, וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי – מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְמֵינַס נַפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the two-sided question from step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Picks one side of the question and shows it still makes sense
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Someone with no other road is helpless and deserves no special praise.
steps.terutzMaskana: He has no choice about the road, but he still must force himself not to look. That self-control is what is praised.

steps.title: How long a scholar's undershirt and cloak should be
steps.stepSummary: רבי בנאה tells רבי יוחנן that a תלמיד חכם's undershirt must be long enough to cover his body, and his cloak must be long enough to cover the undershirt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן asked רבי בנאה: How should a תלמיד חכם's undershirt be? Long enough that his skin does not show below it. How should a תלמיד חכם's cloak be? Long enough that a טפח of his undershirt does not show below it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: more teachings from רבי בנאה, this time about how a תלמיד חכם should dress. רבי יוחנן asks and רבי בנאה answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two layers of clothing. The inner one (חלוק) must hide his skin, and the outer one (טלית) must hide the inner one. The idea is that a תלמיד חכם should always look modest and neat.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מֵרַבִּי בְּנָאָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan asked Rabbi Bena'a:
The undershirt of a Torah scholar, how should it be?
Any one long enough that his skin is not seen from beneath it.
phrases.notes: This is רבי בנאה's answer; the גמרא just gives it without saying "he answered."

phrases.english: The cloak of a Torah scholar, how should it be?

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁאֵין חֲלוּקוֹ נִרְאֶה מִתַּחְתָּיו טֶפַח.
phrases.english: Any one long enough that a handbreadth of his undershirt is not seen from beneath it.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מֵרַבִּי בְּנָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings more teachings from רבי בנאה, who was quoted in step 6 about the courtyard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The undershirt must hide the skin, and the cloak must hide the undershirt.

steps.title: How a scholar's table should be set
steps.stepSummary: רבי בנאה describes a תלמיד חכם's table: two-thirds covered with a cloth, one-third bare with dishes and vegetables on it, and the ring on the outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: How should a תלמיד חכם's table be? Two-thirds covered with a cloth and one-third uncovered, with dishes and vegetables on the uncovered part. Its ring goes on the outside.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the third question in the same series. רבי בנאה explains how a תלמיד חכם's table should be arranged.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The table has a ring that was used to hang it up. רבי בנאה says the ring goes on the outside, away from the person eating. This detail about the ring sets up the next step, where a ברייתא disagrees.

keyTerms.meaning: Its ring, used to hang the table

phrases.english: The table of a Torah scholar, how should it be?
Two-thirds covered with a cloth,
and one-third uncovered,
and on it are dishes and vegetables.
phrases.notes: "On it" means on the uncovered third.

phrases.english: And its ring is on the outside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same list of questions to רבי בנאה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two-thirds covered, one-third bare with food, and the ring on the outside.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the ring goes on the inside
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that a ברייתא says the opposite: the ring goes on the inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches that its ring goes on the inside!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last detail of רבי בנאה's teaching. A ברייתא says the ring belongs on the inside, not the outside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two sources give opposite instructions about the same ring. The גמרא needs to explain how both can be right.

keyTerms.meaning: But it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: its ring is on the inside!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ring rule from step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that the ring goes on the outside
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא directly says the opposite, so the two sources contradict each other.

steps.title: It depends on whether a child is there
steps.stepSummary: The ring goes outside when a child is present, so the child won't play with it, and inside when no child is present.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult. This source is when there is a child, and that source is when there is no child.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two sources are talking about different situations. One is when a child is around and one is when no child is around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a child at the table, the ring is kept outside, away from the child, who might pull it and tip the table over. With no child there, the ring can go inside. So both rules are correct, each in its own case.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is where there is a child,
phrases.notes: "This" is רבי בנאה's rule, where the ring goes outside; "that" in the next line is the ברייתא, where it goes inside.

phrases.english: that is where there is no child.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two sources seem to give conflicting rules for every table.
steps.terutzMaskana: Outside when a child is present; inside when there is none.

steps.title: Second answer: it depends on whether a waiter is there
steps.stepSummary: Both sources might be about a table with no child. The difference is whether a waiter is serving: with a waiter the ring goes inside so he won't bump into it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say both sources are about a case with no child, and still there is no difficulty. This one is where there is a waiter, and that one is where there is no waiter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another way to settle the contradiction. This time the deciding factor is a waiter serving the meal, not a child.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a waiter walking around the table, the ring goes inside so he does not bump into it. With no waiter, the ring can go outside. This answer works even if no child is ever at the table.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say instead (introduces another answer)
Both this one and that one

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
both this and that are where there is no child;
and it is not difficult:
this is where there is a waiter,
phrases.notes: Here "this" is the ברייתא that puts the ring inside, so the waiter won't knock into it.

phrases.english: that is where there is no waiter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, different answer to the contradiction in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases with a different factor
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe the child is the only thing that changes the rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even with no child, a waiter's presence decides it: inside with a waiter, outside without one.

steps.title: Third answer: it depends on day or night
steps.stepSummary: Both sources might be about a table with a waiter. During the day the ring can go outside because the waiter can see it; at night it goes inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say both sources are about a case with a waiter, and still there is no difficulty. This one is during the day, and that one is at night.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third way to settle the contradiction. Even with a waiter present, it depends on whether the meal is by day or by night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By day the waiter can see the ring and walk around it, so it can stay outside. At night he can't see it and might bump into it, so it goes inside. Each answer narrows the case a little more.
steps.whatToRemember: The two sources about the ring don't really disagree. Each fits a different situation: a child present or not, a waiter present or not, or day versus night. The goal is always to keep the table safe from being knocked over.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
both this and that are where there is a waiter;
and it is not difficult:
this is by day,
phrases.notes: "This" is the rule that puts the ring outside, since the waiter can see it in daylight.

phrases.english: that is by night.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא דְּאִיכָּא שַׁמָּעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a third answer, building on the waiter case from step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by time of day
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe whenever there is a waiter, the ring must always go inside.
steps.terutzMaskana: With a waiter, the ring goes outside by day and inside by night.

steps.title: Turning to the table of an unlearned person
steps.stepSummary: Having described the neat table of a תלמיד חכם, the statement now begins to describe the table of an עם הארץ by saying it is 'like' something.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the table of an unlearned person is like...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a contrast. It has finished with the תלמיד חכם's table and now starts to say what an עם הארץ's table resembles, with the comparison coming right after this line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 11–15 were all about the orderly table of a תלמיד חכם. The word 'וְשֶׁל' signals a switch to a different kind of person, and 'דּוֹמֶה' tells us a comparison is coming. This line on its own does not finish the thought.

keyTerms.meaning: An unlearned person, someone not careful in Torah knowledge and its refined ways
Is like, resembles. It introduces a comparison

steps.confusionAlert: Don't stop here thinking the sentence is complete. The word דּוֹמֶה ('is like') needs the next words to tell you what it is like.

phrases.english: But the table of an unlearned person is like
phrases.notes: 'Table' isn't written here. The גמרא assumes it from the earlier steps about the תלמיד חכם's table.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the back-and-forth about where the ring goes (steps 12–15), the גמרא returns to רבי בנאה's description from step 11 and moves from the תלמיד חכם's table to the עם הארץ's table.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The table of an עם הארץ is compared to something different from the orderly table of a תלמיד חכם. The comparison itself follows in the next words.
